subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Laws as agreements that serve people [Actor]
passage: Monday. The notice on the hostel board said the gate would close at eight for the women's wing and at eleven for the men's. Gargi, a second-year law student, read it twice. Her roommate Neelam shrugged. "Seniors just climb the back wall." Gargi shook her head. "Breaking it doesn't fix it. Swallowing it doesn't either." Thursday. In jurisprudence class the professor called law a social contract: people accept limits because the limits protect them. Gargi wrote in her margin, "Who does the eight o'clock rule protect? Whose rights does it cut?" That night she drafted a petition asking for one closing time for every wing, with safety ideas attached, and forty students signed. The next Tuesday the warden and the student council heard her out. They agreed to a formal review and set ten o'clock for all wings until then. Neelam grinned. "You never climbed a wall, and you still moved the gate."

qa.q: What time would the gate close for the women's wing, according to the notice?
qa.a: At eight.

qa.q: What was Gargi thinking when she wrote in her margin during jurisprudence class?
qa.a: She was testing the rule against its purpose, asking whose protection the eight o'clock rule served and whose rights it cut.

qa.q: Which choice turned things around for Gargi, and why did it work?
qa.a: Drafting a petition with safety ideas and gathering forty signatures; it gave the warden and council a fair way to review the rule instead of facing defiance.

qa.q: How might Neelam see Gargi's approach, given Neelam's first suggestion?
qa.a: Neelam first assumed the only way round the rule was climbing the back wall, so Neelam is struck that Gargi changed it without breaking it.

grounding: A law student judges a hostel rule by whose rights and welfare it serves and seeks change through a petition and formal review rather than obeying it blindly or breaking it.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Laws as agreements that serve people [Actor]
passage: "Tanvir, sit with your Nani a minute. You asked why I get cross when people say rules are rules. When I was twenty, the girls in my college called me Sudha the stubborn. Our library shut its doors to day scholars at five. Many of my friends had no electric light at home. Some wanted to slip in with borrowed hostel cards. Others said, 'The principal decided, so that is that.' I sat under the neem tree and asked myself: a rule is a promise we make to each other so that everyone is safer or better off. Whom was this one helping now? It was made when there were few books and fewer guards. So I wrote it all down, collected signatures, and asked the student union to put it before the college council. They voted. The library stayed open till eight for everyone. That, beta, is how you mend a rule."

qa.q: Until what time did the library stay open after the council voted?
qa.a: Till eight, for everyone.

qa.q: What was Sudha thinking as she sat under the neem tree?
qa.a: She saw a rule as a promise people make to each other for safety or welfare, so she wondered whom this old rule was still helping.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sudha's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Instead of slipping in with borrowed cards or accepting the principal's word, she wrote it down, gathered signatures and went to the college council, so a fair vote changed the rule.

qa.q: What might Tanvir take from hearing this story from Nani?
qa.a: Tanvir learns why Nani gets cross at 'rules are rules': a rule can be questioned and mended through a fair process, not only obeyed or dodged.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how, at twenty, she judged a library rule by whose welfare it served and changed it through signatures and a council vote rather than evasion or blind acceptance.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Laws as agreements that serve people [Actor]
passage: The notice gave vendors two days to clear the lane outside the polytechnic gate. Shankar, who ran the tea stall there to pay his fees, stared at it. "Let's block the road tomorrow. Or I stay put and they can fine me." Madhav, a third-year student, felt the same heat rise, but he made himself think it through. "The lane was jammed. An ambulance got stuck here last month. The rule is meant to protect people. It just forgets the people it pushes out." The ward committee would meet at ten the next morning. That night the power went off across the colony, so the two of them went stall to stall with a torch, noting who sold what and where each cart could fit. By morning they had twenty-two names and a sketch of a vending strip beside the bus stop. The committee argued for an hour, then agreed to try the strip for three months.

qa.q: Why did Shankar run the tea stall?
qa.a: To pay his fees.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling and thinking when he read the notice?
qa.a: He felt the same anger as Shankar, but he saw that a rule meant to protect people, after an ambulance got stuck, still forgot the vendors it pushed out.

qa.q: Which choice made the difference before the ten o'clock meeting?
qa.a: Going stall to stall with a torch to list names and sketch a vending strip; it gave the committee a fair option that kept the lane clear and the vendors working.

qa.q: How might Shankar's view of the rule change between the notice and the committee's decision?
qa.a: At first Shankar wanted to block the road or take a fine; seeing the trial strip agreed, he may feel rules can make room for people like him when they are argued fairly.

grounding: A student weighs a vending ban's safety purpose against vendors' welfare and pushes for change through the ward committee rather than defiance or silent compliance.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage: Staff note, 14 March. Written by Indu Rao, head of English. Vaibhav has applied our late-work rule all term without fuss: anything handed in after the deadline scores zero. On Monday he came to me with a written objection instead. A Class 9 student had missed the deadline during the week her father was in hospital, and the zero would drop her below the scholarship line. He did not quietly change the mark, and he did not complain in the staffroom. He asked for the case to go to the academic committee, with the rule's purpose, fairness to everyone, set out beside the harm to this student. The committee met on Wednesday and kept the zero, saying exceptions need a written policy first. Vaibhav said, "I disagree, but it was heard properly." Then he asked to help draft that policy. I have put him on the review group.

qa.q: What score does work handed in after the deadline get?
qa.a: Anything handed in after the deadline scores zero.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav's remark after the committee meeting suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He still thought the decision was wrong, but he respected that the case had been heard properly, so he could accept it without bitterness.

qa.q: Which choice did Vaibhav make on Monday, and what did it avoid?
qa.a: He took a written objection to the academic committee, setting the rule's purpose beside the harm; it avoided both quietly changing the mark and grumbling in the staffroom.

qa.q: How does Indu seem to see Vaibhav after the committee's decision?
qa.a: Indu seems to trust him more, since Indu put him on the review group after he accepted the ruling and offered to help draft a policy.

grounding: A young teacher follows the late-work rule in ordinary cases, formally objects when it would harm a student, and accepts the committee's ruling against him.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage: Friday night. Long day. Nine disconnection orders this week, and I signed eight without blinking, because the rule is clear and those bills really were months overdue. Number nine was Gulmohar Towers. The residents paid every month. The builder pocketed the money. Cutting their water punishes forty families for someone else's cheating. Rashmi half-joked that I should just lose the file for a while. I didn't. I wrote a formal objection to the review board and attached every payment receipt the residents had given me. The board met at four. Rashmi came along for support. They voted to go ahead with the cut, but to send a tanker every day until the case against the builder is settled. Not what I wanted. Still, they read each receipt and gave their reasons in writing. I'll sign the order on Monday. And I'll write to them again next month if nothing moves. - Jeevan

qa.q: How many disconnection orders did Jeevan have this week?
qa.a: Nine disconnection orders.

qa.q: How can you tell Jeevan had mixed feelings about the board's decision?
qa.a: Jeevan writes 'Not what I wanted' yet notes that the board read each receipt and gave reasons, so there is disappointment mixed with respect.

qa.q: What choice did Jeevan make about the Gulmohar Towers file, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Jeevan wrote a formal objection with the receipts instead of losing the file, so the forty families' case was weighed openly.

qa.q: How might the forty families at Gulmohar Towers be affected by Jeevan's objection, even though the cut goes ahead?
qa.a: They still lose piped water, but a daily tanker now reaches them, and someone inside the office has argued their case in writing.

grounding: A young utility engineer applies the disconnection rule in ordinary cases, lodges a formal objection where it would punish innocent residents, and accepts the board's reasoned ruling.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
Suraj: canteen?
Naveen: in 10. finishing my objection for the safety committee
Suraj: the water-break thing? just let the loaders drink when they want, nobody checks bay 3
Naveen: I've kept the break schedule for two years. it's a good rule mostly, stops the line from stalling
Naveen: but in this heat two fixed breaks aren't enough. Arif nearly fainted on Tuesday
Suraj: so bend it quietly
Naveen: then it's still wrong for every other shift. I want it changed properly
Suraj: ok ok. good luck
Next evening
Suraj: verdict??
Naveen: they said no to breaks whenever you want. added one extra fixed break for the summer months
Suraj: that's it?? 😠
Naveen: less than I asked. but they called Arif in, checked the heat log and explained why they said no
Naveen: I'll follow it and push again after summer 👍
Suraj: you're too patient
Naveen: maybe. but next time they'll know I play fair

qa.q: How many fixed breaks were there before the committee's decision?
qa.a: Two fixed breaks.

qa.q: What was Naveen thinking when Suraj suggested bending the rule quietly?
qa.a: Naveen thought a quiet exception would leave the rule wrong for every other shift, and wanted it changed properly instead.

qa.q: What was the key choice Naveen made after the committee's ruling?
qa.a: Naveen accepted the extra summer break though it was less than asked, and planned to push again after summer, keeping faith with the process.

qa.q: Why might Suraj react more angrily than Naveen to the verdict?
qa.a: Suraj only saw the result falling short, while Naveen saw that the committee heard Arif, checked the heat log and gave reasons.

grounding: A young supervisor keeps the break schedule in ordinary times, formally objects when heat endangers workers, and accepts a partial ruling from a fair committee.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Person affected by a fair process feels respected [Receiver]
passage: The cooling plant hummed behind the cooperative office while Trisha waited on the bench, her complaint folded in her lap. She had run the morning milk collection for three years, and the in-charge post had gone to Mohan, who joined after her. Deepika, the manager, called her in and spread three sheets on the table. "These are the marks the panel gave, and the reasons," she said. Mohan's testing record was stronger; he had passed the quality course that Trisha kept postponing. Trisha argued that she knew every farmer by name. Deepika wrote that down. "It counts. It just wasn't enough this time. The next post opens in March, and the course runs in January." Walking home past the tractor repair shed, Trisha still felt the sting. But nobody had brushed her off, and she could see exactly why. She signed up for the January course that evening.

qa.q: How long had Trisha run the morning milk collection?
qa.a: For three years.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling as she walked home past the tractor repair shed?
qa.a: She still felt the sting of losing the post, but also respected, because nobody had brushed her off and the reasons were clear.

qa.q: What did Trisha decide that evening, and why was it a turning point?
qa.a: She signed up for the January course, turning a lost post into a clear path toward the March opening.

qa.q: Why might Deepika have written down Trisha's point about knowing every farmer?
qa.a: Deepika wanted Trisha to see that her argument was weighed and not dismissed, so she could trust the panel even though the result went against her.

grounding: An employee who loses a promotion is shown the panel's marks and reasons, feels respected despite the outcome, and trusts the process enough to prepare for the next round.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Person affected by a fair process feels respected [Receiver]
passage: Soo-ah had rehearsed her case on the tram: her ride to the Melbourne studio took ninety minutes each way, and two days at home would give her back six hours a week. Leila from people operations met her in the small glass room with a printout of the policy and Soo-ah's own email. "I read this twice," Leila said. "Here's what the panel weighed." She went through it point by point: clients came in on fixed days, junior designers needed seniors nearby, and three other requests were being judged by the same rules. The answer was no, for now. "The policy is reviewed in October. Your email can go into that review, with your name on it if you want." Soo-ah was quiet, then nodded. On the tram home she texted her sister: "Didn't get it. But they actually listened. Weird how much that helps."

qa.q: How long did Soo-ah's ride to the studio take each way?
qa.a: Ninety minutes each way.

qa.q: What does Soo-ah's text to her sister reveal about how she felt?
qa.a: She was disappointed but felt genuinely listened to, which eased the sting of the no.

qa.q: What could Soo-ah choose to do before the October review?
qa.a: She could let her email go into the review with her name on it and address the points about client days and junior designers, making her case stronger.

qa.q: Why might Leila have brought Soo-ah's own email to the meeting?
qa.a: Leila wanted to show it had been read closely, so Soo-ah would see her request was weighed by the same rules as everyone else's.

grounding: An employee whose request is refused feels respected and trusts the policy review because her case was read closely and answered with open reasons.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Person affected by a fair process feels respected [Receiver]
passage: The staff room of the city library smelled of old paper and filter coffee when Rafiq pinned the rota to the board. Jahnavi had complained in writing that she worked more Sundays than anyone. He had not waved it away. Now, in front of all six staff, he went through the year month by month. Jahnavi had worked eleven Sundays. Mercy had worked nine, but had also covered six late evenings that Jahnavi never did. "On balance it's close to even," Rafiq said. "So the rota stays. But you were right that nobody could see this before. From now on the tally goes up here every month." Jahnavi felt her face warm; she had been wrong about the numbers. Yet nobody laughed, and her complaint had changed something. When the next swap request came, she filled in the form without grumbling.

qa.q: How many Sundays had Jahnavi worked?
qa.a: Eleven Sundays.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when her face warmed?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed at being wrong about the numbers, but also relieved that nobody laughed and her complaint was taken seriously.

qa.q: What choice did Rafiq make that turned a lost complaint into something useful?
qa.a: He showed the full year's record openly and agreed to post the tally every month, so the complaint changed how the rota is shared.

qa.q: How might Mercy see the open rota meeting?
qa.a: Mercy's late evenings finally became visible to everyone, so Mercy may feel that all kinds of extra work are now counted fairly.

grounding: A library worker whose complaint is checked openly and answered with reasons feels respected despite losing, and trusts the rota more.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
Subject: Something I saw at work

Hi Vijay,

Remember how I used to say there are two kinds of people at work, the ones who follow orders and the ones who roll their eyes at every rule? This week I saw a third kind. Management announced that anyone taking leave in the audit quarter would lose their bonus, even for a family emergency. Most of us grumbled at lunch and said nothing upstairs. Kalpana did something else. She wrote to HR, copied our manager, and asked for it to go to the staff council. She didn't mock the policy, and she didn't skip work in protest. At the council she said, "I want this firm to do well. That's why I'm raising this." They agreed to exempt emergencies. I always thought loyalty meant keeping quiet. Apparently not.

Write soon,
Preeti

qa.q: What did management say would happen to anyone taking leave in the audit quarter?
qa.a: They would lose their bonus, even for a family emergency.

qa.q: What does Preeti now believe about loyalty, and what shows it?
qa.a: Preeti writes 'I always thought loyalty meant keeping quiet. Apparently not', showing that Kalpana's open objection now looks loyal too.

qa.q: Which choice made Kalpana's objection work where the lunchtime grumbling did not?
qa.a: She wrote to HR, copied the manager and asked for the staff council, so the concern reached people who could change the policy.

qa.q: How might the manager copied on Kalpana's email see her?
qa.a: The manager may see Kalpana as someone who cares about the firm, because she raised the issue openly and said she wanted it to do well.

grounding: A colleague watches a peer challenge an unfair leave policy through HR and the staff council, and sees that loyalty and principle can go together.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage: Neelam leaned toward the microphone. "So, Swati, you want the story? I was two years into the night desk at the newspaper. The editor brought in a rule: no byline for anyone with under a year's service, even if they wrote the whole piece. Most juniors shrugged. One senior, Tomas, called it feudal and started leaving his own byline off in protest. Then there was Farzana. She'd written three front-page stories without her name. She didn't sulk, didn't sneer. She wrote a proposal for the editorial board: full bylines for staff, a 'with' credit for trainees. She presented it at the monthly meeting, calm, with dates and page numbers in hand. The board said yes. What stuck with me? She walked into that meeting wearing the paper's lanyard she was so proud of. I'd thought you had to choose, the paper or your principles. Farzana didn't."

qa.q: How many front-page stories had Farzana written without her name?
qa.a: Three front-page stories.

qa.q: What did Neelam come to believe after watching Farzana at the meeting?
qa.a: Neelam realised you don't have to choose between the paper and your principles, since Farzana was proud of the paper and still objected.

qa.q: What set Farzana's response apart from Tomas's, and why did it succeed?
qa.a: Tomas called the rule feudal and dropped his byline, while Farzana brought a calm proposal with dates and pages to the board, giving them something they could accept.

qa.q: How might the trainees be affected by the board's decision?
qa.a: They now get a 'with' credit instead of no name at all, so their work becomes visible because one person objected properly.

grounding: A colleague recalls a peer who challenged an unfair byline rule through a proposal to the board, without sneering, and learns loyalty and principle can coexist.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage: My name's Yash. I sit two desks from Aadhya at the logistics firm, so I saw most of it. The new policy said drivers who reported a vehicle fault after hours would lose half a day's pay. Aadhya read the email, went still, and opened a blank document. I assumed she'd forward it round with a sarcastic line; I had one half-typed myself. She didn't. By evening she had a two-page note for the operations committee: how many faults were found after hours last year, what happens when drivers hide them, and an idea for a night reporting line. She sent it through the proper form and told our manager face to face that she had done so. I can't say what she felt. She looked calm, maybe tired. I deleted my half-typed forward that evening. A fortnight later the committee dropped the pay cut.

qa.q: What would drivers who reported a vehicle fault after hours lose under the new policy?
qa.a: Half a day's pay.

qa.q: What does Yash's deleted forward suggest about how Yash's thinking changed?
qa.a: Yash had planned to mock the policy, but watching Aadhya's careful note made sarcasm feel small beside a proper objection.

qa.q: What steps did Aadhya take that made her objection work?
qa.a: She wrote a two-page note with last year's figures and a night reporting idea, used the proper form, and told the manager face to face.

qa.q: How might the drivers see the committee's decision?
qa.a: The drivers no longer risk losing pay for reporting faults, so they can report them honestly instead of hiding them.

grounding: A colleague watches a peer object to an unfair pay policy through the proper committee without sarcasm or rule-breaking, and drops their own mockery.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage: My name is Mridul, and last year I became the youngest secretary our housing society had ever had. Within a month I had a fight on my hands. The rule said no delivery riders past the gate after nine at night. Mrs Pillai on the fourth floor wanted it kept; she'd had a scare with a stranger on the stairs. Sumit, who works nights at a call centre, had been walking down to the gate for food every evening and eating at midnight. Both had a point. So I didn't pick a side over tea. I wrote both concerns on one sheet: residents' safety, and fair access for people on odd hours. I asked everyone affected to come to the general meeting, and I followed the bylaws: notice, agenda, a vote. We agreed on a pickup shelf at the gate with a guard's log. It isn't perfect. We'll look at it again in six months.

qa.q: What did the old rule say about delivery riders?
qa.a: No delivery riders past the gate after nine at night.

qa.q: What was Mridul thinking in choosing not to pick a side over tea?
qa.a: Mridul believed both Mrs Pillai and Sumit had a point, so a private decision would be unfair to one of them.

qa.q: Which step in Mridul's handling helped both sides accept the pickup shelf?
qa.a: Writing both concerns on one sheet and bringing everyone affected to a properly noticed meeting and vote, so each side was heard and the result was shared.

qa.q: How might Mrs Pillai feel about the pickup shelf with a guard's log?
qa.a: Mrs Pillai may feel her scare was taken seriously, since strangers still stop at the gate and a guard keeps a record.

grounding: A young society secretary lays out safety and access concerns, invites those affected to a proper meeting and vote, and keeps the rule open to improvement.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage: Chief warden's note, 9 November. Written by Bhavna Menon. Minakshi, our assistant warden, handled the lights-out dispute this week, and I want it on record. The hostel rule says rooms go dark at half past ten. Before the semester exams, a group of third-years asked to study till one. The first-years' rooms share walls with theirs, and the younger students need their sleep. Minakshi neither granted nor refused it on the spot. She listed on the notice board what was at stake: rest for the younger students, study time for the older ones, and the safety reasons behind the original rule. She called a residents' meeting and let both years speak without interruption. Then she used the hostel committee's amendment form, as the handbook requires. The committee approved the ground-floor reading room staying open till one during exams. Minakshi has asked to review the rule every semester. I have agreed.

qa.q: What time do rooms go dark under the hostel rule?
qa.a: At half past ten.

qa.q: What might Minakshi have been worried about when the third-years asked to study till one?
qa.a: She likely worried that saying yes would cost the first-years their sleep through the shared walls, while saying no would hurt the older students' exam study.

qa.q: What small step in Minakshi's process helped everyone accept the result?
qa.a: Letting both years speak without interruption at a residents' meeting, then using the amendment form, made the decision feel fair to both sides.

qa.q: How might the first-years see the new reading-room arrangement?
qa.a: They keep quiet rooms at night while the third-years study downstairs, so they may feel their needs counted as much as the seniors'.

grounding: An assistant warden facing a lights-out conflict lays out the welfare at stake, lets both groups speak, uses the agreed amendment procedure and plans regular review.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage: Tuesday, 11 pm. Big day. Our academy rule: miss two practices and you're off the tournament list. Jyoti missed two last week, looking after her little brother while her mother was in hospital. Half the team said rules are rules; the other half said scrap the rule altogether. My stomach was in knots all morning. I didn't want to decide it alone in the office. So after practice I sat the team down and wrote on the whiteboard: fairness to those who turned up, and a player's right not to be punished for a family crisis. Everyone spoke, even Jyoti, who said she would accept whatever we decided. Then I did it properly and took it to the academy director with the team's notes. Result: Jyoti stays in, and practice missed for a family emergency will now be reviewed case by case. I'll sleep better knowing it's written down. - Ankita

qa.q: Why did Jyoti miss two practices last week?
qa.a: She was looking after her little brother while her mother was in hospital.

qa.q: How can you tell Ankita felt uneasy before the team meeting?
qa.a: Ankita writes of a stomach in knots all morning and not wanting to decide it alone in the office.

qa.q: What choice did Ankita make after practice, and why did it help?
qa.a: Ankita sat the team down, wrote both concerns on the whiteboard and let everyone speak, so what went to the director reflected the whole team.

qa.q: What is it like for Jyoti to hear the team argue about the rule?
qa.a: Jyoti is exposed and probably anxious, yet says she'll accept whatever they decide, which suggests she trusts the process to be fair.

grounding: A young coach facing a rule conflict sets out fairness and a player's welfare, lets the team speak, follows the academy's procedure and gets the rule improved.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Monday. Maria, five, pushed Simran off the swing. The teacher frowned, and Maria went pale. "Am I bad now? Will I get a punishment?" Wednesday. Simran grabbed Maria's crayon. Maria's hand went up, then she looked at the teacher's desk and dropped it. "No hitting," she whispered. "Teacher gets angry." Friday. At home, Nani asked Maria why hitting is wrong. "Because you get punished," Maria said firmly. "That's the rule." "And if nobody saw?" Maria thought very hard, swinging her legs. "Then it's still the rule, Nani. Rules are just there."

qa.q: What did Maria do on Monday?
qa.a: She pushed Simran off the swing.

qa.q: What was Maria worried about when the teacher frowned?
qa.a: She worried she was bad now and that she would get a punishment.

qa.q: What choice did Maria make on Wednesday, and what was it based on?
qa.a: She dropped her raised hand instead of hitting Simran, because she expected the teacher to get angry.

qa.q: What might change if Nani asked Maria how Simran felt after the push?
qa.a: Maria might begin to notice that hitting hurts Simran, not only that it makes adults angry.

grounding: A five-year-old explains that hitting is wrong because you get punished and treats the rule as simply there, judging right by adult anger.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Rain kept the whole kindergarten indoors, and the teacher had stepped out to fetch towels. Omkar snatched Hemant's toy truck. Hemant's fist came up. Then he looked at the door. It was empty. He still stopped. "Hitting is bad," he told Omkar in a loud whisper. "Why?" said Omkar. "'Cause Miss gets angry and you sit in the corner chair." "But Miss isn't here." Hemant's forehead crinkled. He looked at the door again, then at the corner chair, as if the chair itself might tell on him. "The corner knows," he said, and put both hands behind his back.

qa.q: Why had the teacher stepped out?
qa.a: To fetch towels.

qa.q: What does Hemant's look at the corner chair suggest he believed?
qa.a: He seemed to believe punishment was simply part of the world, so it could catch him even with Miss away.

qa.q: What could Miss do when she comes back to build on Hemant's choice?
qa.a: She could praise him for keeping his hands back and ask how Omkar might feel if hit, so his reason grows beyond the corner chair.

qa.q: Why might Omkar question Hemant's reason?
qa.a: Omkar noticed Miss was not in the room, so the threat of the corner seemed empty to Omkar.

grounding: A kindergartner holds back from hitting because the teacher gets angry and the corner punishes, treating the rule as a fixed fact even when no adult is present.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Kiran, five, came up three floors in the lift, crying. "Salma hit me! Ammi, she's very bad now. Watchman uncle will tell her mummy and she'll get a big scolding." Ammi wiped his face with her dupatta. "Is hitting wrong only because of the scolding?" Kiran looked at her as if she had asked why the sky was up. "Hitting is wrong because you get punished, Ammi. Everybody knows." "And if nobody scolded her?" He thought about it, then shook his head. "Somebody always scolds."

qa.q: Who did Kiran say would tell Salma's mummy?
qa.a: Watchman uncle.

qa.q: What does Kiran's look at Ammi suggest he thought of her question?
qa.a: He found her question strange, as if the rule about hitting were as plain a fact as the sky being up.

qa.q: What could Ammi try next to help Kiran look beyond the scolding?
qa.a: She could ask how the hit felt to him, so he links hitting with hurt rather than only with punishment.

qa.q: What would change if Ammi had simply promised to get Salma scolded?
qa.a: Kiran would learn even more firmly that right and wrong depend on an adult's anger, instead of starting to think about why hitting hurts.

grounding: A five-year-old says hitting is wrong because you get punished and cannot imagine a world where no one scolds, treating the rule as a fact.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Dhruv's phone buzzed all through dinner in their Bhopal flat: Manoj's birthday, Saturday, cake at the food court at four and a movie at six. Saturday evening was also when Dhruv had promised Papa he would mind the hardware shop from six while Papa went to a wedding. "A good son keeps his word," Papa had said, patting his shoulder, and Dhruv had glowed. Now Manoj wrote, "U better come for the movie. Real friends show up." Dhruv typed, deleted, typed again. He pictured the gang calling him boring, and Manoj's face when the seat stayed empty. He pictured Papa's face if the shutter stayed down. At midnight he sent: "Coming for the cake. Can't do the movie, shop duty." Manoj replied with a thumbs-up. Dhruv lay awake anyway, wondering whether both of them were a little disappointed in him.

qa.q: Where was the cake for Manoj's birthday?
qa.a: At the food court at four.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv glow when Papa patted his shoulder?
qa.a: Being called a good son who keeps his word mattered deeply to him; he wanted Papa's approval.

qa.q: What choice did Dhruv make at midnight, and what was he trying to balance?
qa.a: He chose the cake but not the movie, trying to keep his promise to Papa while still showing up as a loyal friend.

qa.q: How might Manoj read Dhruv's midnight message?
qa.a: Manoj might be glad Dhruv is coming for the cake or a little let down about the movie; the thumbs-up doesn't show which.

grounding: A teenager torn between being a good son and a loyal friend struggles to disappoint either and lies awake over their approval.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: "Ammi, can I eat in my room?" "Since when? Sit. What happened, Imran?" "Nothing." Parveen put down the ladle. "Your face says something." "There's a new boy, Joel. The group decided nobody sits with him. He tried to sit with us and Faisal said the table was full." "Was it?" "No." Imran pushed his rice around. "I wanted to move my bag. But then they'd say I'm not with them. Faisal's been my friend since Class 3." "And what do you want to be, beta?" "A good friend. And a good son. You'd be ashamed if I was mean." "Would I?" "Yes, Ammi." He looked up. "So what do I do when I can't be both?" Parveen sat down beside him. "Tell me what a good friend would do for Joel."

qa.q: What did Faisal say when Joel tried to sit with them?
qa.a: Faisal said the table was full.

qa.q: Why is Imran pushing his rice around instead of eating?
qa.a: He is torn: he wanted to move his bag for Joel but feared the group would think he wasn't with them, and he doesn't want Ammi to be ashamed of him.

qa.q: What choice does Imran face at lunch tomorrow, and what small step could he take?
qa.a: He must choose between the group's approval and fairness to Joel; he could start by moving his bag and saying hello, even if Faisal frowns.

qa.q: What is it like for Joel when Faisal says the table is full?
qa.a: Joel is shut out on purpose and likely feels embarrassed and alone, without knowing Imran wanted to move his bag.

grounding: A teenager who wants to be seen as a loyal friend and a good son finds it hard to go against his group, and talks it through with his mother at home.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: I'm Zeeshan, and last month I did something I'm still turning over. The inter-school quiz and our dance group's final practices fell in the same week. My maths teacher had picked me for the quiz team, and Abbu told everyone at dinner, glowing. But Dilnaz and the others in the group said, "If you leave now, the whole routine falls apart. We're a team." I couldn't bear the thought of them rolling their eyes at me in the corridor. So I dropped the quiz. Dilnaz hugged me and said I was the best friend ever, and for two days I felt warm and safe. Then Abbu asked when the quiz was, and his face fell when I told him. That was when it hit me. I'd tried so hard to be the good friend and the good son that I never once asked what I wanted.

qa.q: Who told everyone at dinner that Zeeshan was picked for the quiz?
qa.a: Abbu.

qa.q: What was Zeeshan afraid of when the dance group asked him to stay?
qa.a: He was afraid the others would roll their eyes at him in the corridor and see him as a bad friend.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Zeeshan, and what could he ask himself next time?
qa.a: Seeing Abbu's face fall; next time he could ask what he himself wants before choosing between the group and the quiz.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel when he learns Zeeshan dropped the quiz?
qa.a: Abbu had been proud enough to announce it at dinner, so he is likely disappointed and perhaps confused about why Zeeshan gave it up.

grounding: A teenage boy gives up a quiz place to keep his friends' approval and later sees he was chasing the roles of good friend and good son over his own wishes.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Rehana: Jyoti, you're the class rep. can you ask sir to excuse me for Thursday's lab? I was at my Nani's funeral in Kanpur
Jyoti: I'm so sorry, Rehana
Jyoti: I'll pass it on. but the rule is below 75 percent attendance you can't sit the exam
Rehana: I know the rule. I'm asking for one exception
Jyoti: if I push for you, what if everyone breaks the rules with a story?
Rehana: it's not a story. it's my Nani
Jyoti: I know. I'm not saying you're lying
Jyoti: rules only hold the class together if they're the same for everyone
Rehana: so a funeral and a movie count the same?
Jyoti: ...that's not what I mean
Rehana: it's what it feels like
Jyoti: I'll forward your message to sir tonight, word for word
Rehana: fine

qa.q: Why did Rehana miss Thursday's lab?
qa.a: Rehana was at Nani's funeral in Kanpur.

qa.q: What does Jyoti's reply '...that's not what I mean' suggest Jyoti is feeling?
qa.a: Jyoti seems caught off guard and uneasy, sensing that the strict rule treats a funeral like a movie, which Jyoti never intended.

qa.q: What could Jyoti do next that keeps the rule fair and still helps Rehana?
qa.a: Jyoti could forward the request with its reason and ask the teacher whether there is a proper process for bereavement, instead of assuming no exception is possible.

qa.q: What is it like for Rehana to hear 'what if everyone breaks the rules with a story'?
qa.a: Rehana feels a real loss is being treated as a possible excuse, which hurts deeply while grieving.

grounding: A class representative insists rules must be the same for everyone and asks what if everyone broke them, which keeps order but is hard on a grieving classmate.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: The ration shop in Chandpur opened at eight, and by nine the queue curled past the well. Nazia, twenty and three months into her job as the shop's record keeper, kept the register the way she had been trained: every card holder signs for themselves. Bidisha reached the counter holding her grandmother's card. "Thamma can't walk since the fall. I've brought a letter from the pradhan." Nazia's pen stopped. She liked this rule; it had ended the days when grain vanished under other people's names. "If I make one exception, everyone will bring a letter. What if everyone broke the rules? The whole system falls apart." Bidisha's eyes filled. "So she doesn't eat this month?" The people behind shifted and muttered. Nazia looked at the register, then at the letter, and felt the ground under her rule move a little.

qa.q: What did Bidisha bring from the pradhan?
qa.a: A letter.

qa.q: Why did Nazia's pen stop when Bidisha reached the counter?
qa.a: She believed in the rule because it had ended grain vanishing under other names, and she feared one exception would bring everyone with a letter.

qa.q: What could Nazia do next that respects both the rule and Bidisha's grandmother?
qa.a: She could ask her supervisor whether there is an approved way to serve a card holder who cannot walk, instead of refusing outright or bending the register alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Bidisha to hear 'What if everyone broke the rules?'
qa.a: Bidisha feels her grandmother's real need is being treated as a threat to the system, and fears Thamma will go without grain this month.

grounding: A young record keeper defends a strict signing rule as the thing holding the system together, which protects order but is hard on a rare genuine exception.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: At twelve minutes past six the sun dropped behind the hills outside the university library in Cape Town, and Sami unwrapped three dates at a corner desk. Lindiwe, twenty and on her evening shift at the front desk, walked over at once. "Sorry. No food in the reading room. It's on every door." "I've been fasting since dawn," Sami said quietly. "It's three dates. I'll be out of the way." Lindiwe hesitated. She believed in the rule; last year mice had chewed through a whole shelf of journals. "If I let you, the next person brings chips, then pizza. What if everyone broke the rules for their own good reason?" Sami wrapped the dates up again and went outside to eat on the cold steps. Lindiwe returned to the desk and stamped books a little harder than she needed to.

qa.q: Why did Lindiwe believe in the no-food rule?
qa.a: Last year mice had chewed through a whole shelf of journals.

qa.q: What does Lindiwe stamping the books harder suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She seems uneasy, perhaps guilty, about sending a fasting student out to the cold steps, even though she believes she kept the rule.

qa.q: What could Lindiwe have tried that kept the rule's purpose and still helped Sami?
qa.a: She could have pointed Sami to a spot by the entrance or asked a supervisor about a brief allowance, so the shelves stay safe without shutting Sami out.

qa.q: How might Sami see the rule after eating on the cold steps?
qa.a: Sami may feel the rule was applied without seeing a rare, real need, and may feel less welcome in the library.

grounding: A young library assistant defends a no-food rule with 'what if everyone broke the rules', protecting order but treating a rare, genuine need harshly.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
subtype: Stages are tendencies, not labels on people [Observer]
passage: Siddharth set down his chai and told his cousin, "You know I take the ethics tutorial now, right? Twenty-two and grading people nearly my age. Strange. So there's this student, Pradeep. In the debate on copying assignments, he said flatly, 'Don't copy, because you'll get caught and lose marks.' Classic Kohlberg stage one, I thought, and I nearly wrote him off. Then last week we discussed a clinic that turned away a patient without papers, and Pradeep argued that laws exist to protect people and this one was failing its own purpose. That's miles further along the same ladder. Same student, same month. So I stopped treating the stages like labels stamped on foreheads. They're more like which tools someone reaches for in a particular room. My job is to build rooms where the better tools come out."

qa.q: What did Pradeep say in the debate on copying assignments?
qa.a: 'Don't copy, because you'll get caught and lose marks.'

qa.q: What was Siddharth thinking after Pradeep's argument about the clinic?
qa.a: He realised the same student could reason much further along the ladder in a different situation, so his first judgement of Pradeep had been wrong.

qa.q: What choice did Siddharth make after noticing this, and how might it help his students?
qa.a: He chose to treat the stages as tools people reach for in different rooms and to build discussions that bring out stronger reasoning, rather than labelling students.

qa.q: How might Pradeep have been affected if Siddharth had written him off after the first debate?
qa.a: Pradeep might have been treated as a shallow thinker, and his stronger reasoning about the clinic could have gone unnoticed.

grounding: A young tutor who knows Kohlberg's model sees one student reason at very different levels and treats the stages as tendencies rather than labels on people.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
subtype: Stages are tendencies, not labels on people [Observer]
passage: I've shared a staffroom with Yamini at the degree college for two years, so I noticed when she started jotting notes about Vaibhav. He's the first-year who, in the ethics debate, said a shopkeeper who overcharges should be stopped "because the police will fine him." A week later, in a case about a friend asking to copy his project, he refused because "the whole class trusts the teacher to be fair, and copying breaks that." Yamini read both lines aloud to me and laughed. "Same boy, two different levels in one week." Some colleagues rank students by these stages as if they were marks. She doesn't. She told me the model is a map of how thinking can grow, not a scorecard of goodness. I can't say what she really feels about him. But she gave him the hardest case in the next debate.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav say an overcharging shopkeeper should be stopped?
qa.a: "Because the police will fine him."

qa.q: What does Yamini's laugh suggest about how she felt reading both lines?
qa.a: She seemed delighted and curious to see the same student reason at two different levels in one week.

qa.q: What choice did Yamini make for the next debate, and why might it help Vaibhav?
qa.a: She gave him the hardest case, which invites the stronger reasoning he showed about trust instead of boxing him at the lower level.

qa.q: How does the narrator's view of Yamini's approach differ from how some colleagues use the stages?
qa.a: The narrator notices that Yamini treats the stages as a map of growth, while some colleagues rank students by them like marks, and the narrator seems to find Yamini's way worth recording.

grounding: A colleague observes a teacher notice one student reasoning at different levels and treat the stage model as a map of growth rather than a ranking of people.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
subtype: Stages are tendencies, not labels on people [Observer]
passage: Monday. Deepika, in her first year teaching the college's values course, read Farida's essay on a stolen exam paper: "Don't take it, you'll be expelled." She pencilled "stage one?" in the margin and felt a little let down. Thursday. In group work, Farida argued that the hostel curfew should be changed by a student vote, because "rules are agreements, and this one ignores students who work evening shifts." Deepika stopped mid-stride between the desks. That was reasoning from a very different place. The following Monday, Deepika rubbed out the pencil note. In her planning book she wrote: "Stages describe the reasoning in a moment, not the person. Farida reaches higher when the question touches her own life." She built the next week's cases around the students' own hostels and part-time jobs.

qa.q: What did Deepika pencil in the margin of Farida's essay?
qa.a: "stage one?"

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she stopped mid-stride on Thursday?
qa.a: She was surprised, realising Farida could reason from a very different place than her essay suggested.

qa.q: What did Deepika change after rubbing out the note, and why is it a good choice?
qa.a: She built the next cases around the students' own hostels and part-time jobs, since Farida reasoned more deeply when the question touched her own life.

qa.q: How might Farida have been affected if the pencil note had stayed?
qa.a: Farida might have been seen and taught as a stage-one thinker, and her stronger reasoning about the curfew could have gone unrecognised.

grounding: A young teacher sees one student reason at different levels over a week and comes to treat the stages as descriptions of reasoning in a moment, not labels on people.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Project log, site 14. Written by Vidya Kulkarni, project head. On Tuesday the contractor wanted the night crew up on the scaffolds during the storm warning. It was within the permit, and the crew leader said his men needed the overtime. Pranav, our junior site engineer, refused to sign the shift sheet. He said, "The permit allows it, but I won't send people up where I wouldn't go myself. Their lives aren't worth less because they are paid by the day." The contractor complained to head office, and Pranav lost his quarterly bonus for delaying the pour. He knew that would happen and did not argue the penalty. I don't think Pranav is some kind of saint; last month he rushed his paperwork like everyone else. But on Tuesday he held a line on principle. I have asked head office to review storm permits.

qa.q: What did the contractor want the night crew to do on Tuesday?
qa.a: To be up on the scaffolds during the storm warning.

qa.q: What did Pranav believe about the day-paid workers, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He believed their lives were worth no less than anyone's, since he said he wouldn't send people up where he wouldn't go himself.

qa.q: What choice did Vidya make after Tuesday, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Vidya asked head office to review storm permits, which could turn one person's stand into a safer rule for every crew.

qa.q: How might the crew leader see Pranav's refusal?
qa.a: The crew leader may be torn: relieved the men stayed safe, yet frustrated that they lost overtime they needed.

grounding: A young engineer acts on a principle of human dignity against a permit and the contractor's wishes and accepts losing his bonus, while the note shows he is not always at that level.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Wednesday night. Today I said no to Deepak for the first time. The flood pictures came in: a mother on a rooftop holding her child's slipper, her face clear, crying. Deepak wanted it for the front page. It is legal; the photographer shot it in a public place, and the whole desk agreed it would sell. I kept thinking: she never agreed to become the face of this. Her grief isn't ours to use. I asked for the picture of the water and the empty street instead. Deepak said I'd lost my nerve and took me off the flood series. That stung more than I expected. I'm no hero; most days I just go along with the desk. But tonight I know exactly why I said no, and I would say it again. - Vikas

qa.q: What did Vikas ask for instead of the mother's picture?
qa.a: The picture of the water and the empty street.

qa.q: What was Vikas thinking while looking at the flood picture?
qa.a: Vikas kept thinking the mother never agreed to become the face of the story, and that her grief wasn't theirs to use.

qa.q: What choice did Vikas make, and what did it cost?
qa.a: Vikas refused to run the mother's photo and offered another, and the cost was being taken off the flood series.

qa.q: How might the mother in the photograph have been affected if the picture had run on the front page?
qa.a: Her private grief would have become a public image without her consent, at one of the worst moments of her life.

grounding: A young journalist acts on a self-chosen principle of dignity against the law's permission and the desk's wishes, accepts the cost, and admits it is not how they usually act.
